title: Integer decode: reject fractional, quoted and out-of-range values for int32/int64 everywhere, including container leaves
canonical: Anywhere an integer is decoded (model field, container element, top-level response) a JSON number for format int32 and for format-less integer must be an integer token inside [-2^31, 2^31-1]; for format int64 inside [-2^63, 2^63-1]. A fractional number (1.5), a quoted string ("5"), a boolean or an out-of-range number raises the SDK SerializationError. Nothing is truncated, coerced, wrapped or rounded. Dynamic languages (python, ruby, php, dart, node, elixir) apply the same range check when a model is constructed or serialised. FORCED exceptions to document in AGENTS.md: (1) node cannot detect int64 values above 2^53 because JSON.parse rounds before the SDK sees them (README already documents it); (2) the literal spelling 1.0 is NOT pinned: node and swift (JSONDecoder) cannot tell it from 1, while the others reject it, so tests must not assert either way. Format-less integer follows int32, as java/kotlin/csharp/go/rust already do through the generator's 'integer' type token.

csharp: canonical (int/long, STJ strict numbers; Order.cs:87).
php: raw and container primitives are strict now (ObjectSerializer.php ~560-600, 'abc'->0 and 1.9->1 are gone; int64 overflow raises OverflowException) but int32 range is not checked (?int, Order.php:30).
python: StrictInt unbounded (order.py:34); container leaves use strict aliases (object_serializer.py:77 _STRICT_LEAF_TYPES) but also unbounded.

node: deserializeLeaf 'integer' = Number.isInteger (object-serializer.ts:883-903) and model constructor typeof+isInteger (order.ts:86-96); no range; int64 above 2^53 rounded.
dart: models 'as int?' (order.dart fromJson) with no range; containers use lazy .cast<String,int>() (store_api.dart:363) so a bad element throws a raw TypeError at element access, outside SerializationException.
go: canonical (int32/int64, order.go:65).

alternatives: (1) Leave range unchecked in the six dynamic languages and document it: rejected, 5 compiled SDKs already reject and the dynamic six then re-send a value the schema forbids (criterion c, and the repo's same-input-same-outcome rule). (2) Treat format-less integer as int64: rejected, would widen java Integer, kotlin Int, csharp int, go int32, rust i32 to 64 bit, a public type break in five shipped SDKs. (3) Make node reject int64 above 2^53 via isSafeInteger: rejected, turns a lossy-but-working call into a hard failure for snowflake-style ids; keep the documented rounding as a forced exception.
rationale: Majority already correct (java, kotlin models, csharp, go, rust, php container leaves). Criteria (c) silent truncation, coercion and bignum acceptance are silent data changes; (d) every language can range-check without a dependency (pydantic Field(ge,le), Int32, guards). The only truly forced pieces are node int64>2^53 and the 1.0 spelling.

title: Schema validation keywords (pattern, min/max length, min/max, multipleOf, min/maxItems) are enforced by NO SDK
canonical: None of the 12 enforces minLength, maxLength, pattern, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum/Maximum, multipleOf, minItems or maxItems client-side, on decode, construction or encode. The server is the authority, exactly as eleven READMEs already say. The keywords may appear in doc comments and (python) as non-enforcing JSON-schema metadata. Python stops emitting them as pydantic Field constraints and its README section is rewritten to match the other eleven.

java, kotlin, csharp, php, ruby, node, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir: no template references these keywords; node README.md:102 says 'not enforced'; all accept any value.
alternatives: Enforce everywhere: rejected. Regex dialects differ (ECMA look-around works in java/js/php/ruby/csharp/python-re but not in Go RE2, Rust regex, pydantic-core), so uniform pattern enforcement needs a per-language translator or a new dependency (criterion d); response-path enforcement turns small server drift into client failures; 11 of 12 READMEs document non-enforcement (criterion b). Enforce only the language-neutral numeric/length/items keywords: rejected, adds 11 implementations for a convenience the server already provides.
rationale: Criteria (b) majority and documented README rule, (d) feasibility; the python-only behaviour also carries two real defects (SyntaxError on a quote in a pattern, import failure on look-around).

title: date-time decode accepts only RFC 3339 (offset required) and never consults the host clock or time zone
canonical: A format: date-time value is decoded only if it matches RFC 3339 date-time: YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS, optional fraction of any length, then Z or +-HH:MM. Offset-less strings, date-only strings, free text ("tomorrow", "Jan 1 2024", "10:00"), US-style dates and epoch numbers raise SerializationError. No path may consult the host zone or the current date. Encode is unchanged (fixed .SSS+00:00). FORCED exception, already documented in AGENTS 'date-time input strictness': swift also accepts a bare yyyy-MM-dd as UTC midnight (one Foundation.Date type for date and date-time); it is host independent.
current_state:
java, kotlin, go, rust, elixir: strict RFC 3339 parsers that never use the host zone (elixir DateTime.from_iso8601 needs an offset).
swift: ISO8601DateFormatter + UTC-pinned DateFormatter + UTC date-only fallback (ObjectSerializer.swift:68-82), host independent; forced date-only acceptance.
csharp: DateTimeOffset.TryParse(text, InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.None) (ObjectSerializer.cs:415-422): offset-less maps to the host offset, accepts "01/02/2024 10:00", "Jan 1 2024", "10:00".
ruby: Time.parse(data.to_s) (object_serializer.rb:388): host-local for offset-less, today's date for "10:00".
node: class-transformer Transform builds new Date(raw) (order.ts:39-50) and deserializeLeaf uses new Date(value) (object-serializer.ts:896): offset-less is host-local.
dart: DateTime.parse(json['shipDate'] as String) (order.dart:85): offset-less becomes a local DateTime.
php: DateTimeNormalizer with RFC3339_EXTENDED (ObjectSerializer.php:95) falls back to new \DateTime($data) (:618/:641), so "tomorrow", "@1700000000" are accepted, offset-less uses php.ini date.timezone, and plain "...:00Z" (no 3-digit fraction) only parses through that lenient fallback.
python: model fields use pydantic AwareDatetime (rejects naive, but lax mode also takes epoch numbers and a space separator); the container/top-level path uses dateutil parse() (object_serializer.py:476, 509, 519), which accepts free text and only rejects the naive result afterwards.
alternatives: Keep platform parsers and document host dependence: rejected, the same wire string yields different instants per machine (criterion c). Also accept offset-less as UTC: rejected, silently invents a zone; RFC 3339 requires the offset and python/elixir/java/go/rust/kotlin already reject.
rationale: (a) RFC 3339 §5.6 and JSON Schema date-time require the offset; (b) six SDKs already strict; (c) no host-dependent instants; (d) a shared pre-gate regex plus the platform parser works in every language with no new dependency.

title: A required property that carries a default (synthetic discriminator default) is filled with that default when absent, in all 12
canonical: When a required property has a default (the synthetic mapping value generated for a oneOf subtype discriminator, e.g. DryFood.foodType = "dry", or a real schema default), decoding a payload that omits the key succeeds and fills the default; an explicit null is still rejected for a non-nullable property. title: An unusable (unparseable) Location behaves exactly like a missing Location: return the 3xx
current_state:
java: IllegalArgumentException from URI.resolve escapes the redirect loop (DefaultApiClient.java:490 resolveLocation -> base.resolve; verified 'Illegal character in authority').

python: urlsplit('http://[bad') raises ValueError('Invalid IPv6 URL') inside _resolve_url (default_api_client.py ~720), uncaught; lenient values are forwarded raw.
ruby: resolve_url rescues to nil and breaks, returning the 3xx (rb:501).
node: new URL(location, currentUrl) throws TypeError (abstract-api-client.ts:335) which the catch maps to NetworkError status 0, and discardBody() already ran.
dart: Uri.resolve FormatException lands in the generic catch -> ApiException(statusCode: 0) (abstract_api_client.dart:271); the 3xx body is drained before the Location check (:256) so even the missing-Location break reads a consumed stream.
go: net/http returns *url.Error 'failed to parse Location header' with resp == nil -> NetworkError status 0.
rust: Url::join(..).ok() -> None -> break, returns the 3xx (default_api_client.rs:295).
swift: URLSession owns Location parsing; Apple platforms complete with the 3xx and never call the redirect delegate (not verified on corelibs).
elixir: resolve_url rescues to nil and returns the response (default_api_client.ex:977).
canonical: Location is 'usable' only if it is non-empty and the platform's RFC 3986 reference resolver accepts it against the current URL. If not, stop the loop and return the 3xx untouched (status, headers, body), exactly like a missing Location; BaseApi then maps it to the ApiError for that status. Order matters: resolve the Location BEFORE draining/cancelling the 3xx body, so the returned response still has its body. A resolvable-but-forbidden scheme (file:, javascript:) stays a typed ApiError carrying the 3xx status, as today in all 12.
rationale: By the error contract a response arrived, so the outcome must be an ApiError/3xx carrying that status, never NetworkError(0) (node, go, dart) nor a leaked library exception (java, kotlin, python). Returning the 3xx matches the 4 SDKs that already do it (php, rust, elixir, ruby) and the missing-Location rule fixed in F088, needs no new error type, and is the safest: nothing is followed, nothing is guessed. Empty Location is folded in because java/kotlin/php/csharp/rust currently resolve '' to the same URL and burn the whole hop budget ('Too many redirects'), whereas node/ruby/dart/python/go already treat it as missing.
alternatives: Raise ApiError(3xx) for a malformed Location. Rejected: it loses the body/headers, needs a new message in 12 languages, and the 4 SDKs that already return the 3xx would have to change. Leave go as NetworkError and document it as forced. Rejected as a default because a thin RoundTripper can reproduce the behaviour; kept only as the fallback if the maintainers refuse the wrapper.

canonical: Proxy credentials authenticate to the proxy, which is the same for every hop, so they belong to the transport, not to the caller's header set. The cross-origin strip removes only caller-supplied credential headers. In the four SDKs that inject Proxy-Authorization as a request header (java, kotlin, swift, dart) the SDK re-applies its own proxyAuthHeader to every redirected request after the strip, with one guard: on a cross-origin hop whose target is https it is NOT re-added (there the header would travel to an unrelated origin inside the TLS tunnel).
rationale: Eight SDKs already authenticate every hop; 407-after-redirect is a functional bug and the finding's fix is local. The https cross-origin guard keeps the fix from handing proxy credentials to an attacker-chosen host on a malicious 302, which would be a silent security weakening.
alternatives: Move credentials to the proxy layer in java/kotlin/swift (java.net.http Authenticator of type PROXY, URLSession proxy challenge). Rejected for now: java needs the JVM-wide jdk.http.auth.tunneling.disabledSchemes property for Basic over CONNECT and Ktor CIO has no proxy-credential API; revisit if header injection proves insufficient (it already cannot authenticate the CONNECT of an https origin).

canonical: timeout is an end-to-end budget measured from the start of sendRequest: connect, TLS, request, every redirect hop, and the response body read all draw from it. Each hop is sent with the remaining budget; if nothing is left before a hop starts, raise the language's NetworkTimeout error (status 0) without sending it. alternatives: Per-hop timeout everywhere. Rejected: contradicts the docs, go/swift/node would need manual redirect loops or per-hop cancellation, and it leaves an unbounded worst case.

current_state:

swift: Foundation URL/URLComponents rewrite '[' ']' (verified on swift 6.2, macOS 15: URL(string:) -> %5B%5D, and URLComponents.percentEncodedQuery traps on them), DefaultApiClient.swift:207.
dart: Uri.parse normalises '[' ']' (abstract_api_client.dart:167; not runnable here).

canonical: BaseApi's encoder keeps the RFC 3986 reserved set literal (OAS allowReserved) and that is the contract. Five SDKs cannot keep every character literal because their URL type owns normalisation: '[' and ']' in python, swift and dart; the apostrophe in node and rust. These are documented FORCED exceptions: the value is preserved (the server percent-decodes %5B/%5D/%27 to the same text) but the bytes differ. Nothing is re-encoded by the SDK itself.
rationale: All three 'avoidable' options in the ledger fail on inspection: pre-encoded urls still go through urllib3's _encode_target, Foundation will not hold '[' in a query, and Dart's Uri has no raw-query setter. The alternative of percent-encoding [ ] ' in all 12 would give identical bytes but break the OAS text (which lists them as literal) in the 7 SDKs that are correct. Value-preserving wire differences are lower risk than changing the encoder in 12 languages.
alternatives: Percent-encode '[', ']' and ''' in the shared encoder for every language so the wire is identical. Rejected: violates OAS allowReserved for the characters that ARE kept literal today, with no benefit to servers. Bypass the URL types (raw http.client / HttpClient.request with a pre-built target). Rejected: large, platform-specific, risks proxy/redirect handling.

canonical: Any parameter declared with `content: application/json` (query, header, path, cookie) is serialized by the SDK's own ObjectSerializer.serialize: wire property names, canonical .SSS+00:00 date-times, null fields omitted, NaN/Infinity rejected, <, > and & literal. The resulting JSON text is then encoded once by the location's normal rule (query component-encoded as for any query value, path segment-encoded, header verbatim after the CR/LF check, cookie encoded). rationale: OpenAPI 3.x says content-encoded parameters carry the media-type serialization of the schema value, so the model's wire form is the SDK's JSON form (criterion a). java, kotlin, dart and swift already route the query case through ObjectSerializer (b). Every language has an ObjectSerializer.serialize entry point, so no dependency is needed (d).
alternatives: Keep each language's stdlib encoder: rejected, 8 of 12 diverge on wire names, dates, null handling or escaping and two swallow errors. Reject content params at generation time: rejected, the 4 correct languages already support them and OpenAPI allows the feature. Fix query only and leave header/path/cookie: rejected, the silent empty-style fallback is a worse failure than the query divergence.

current_state: Re-checked, no format:time anywhere in petstore, so goldens only show the serializers. java: ISO_LOCAL_TIME keeps up to 9 fraction digits (ObjectSerializer.java:167-169). kotlin: NO LocalTime branch, LocalTime matches `is TemporalAccessor -> DATE_TIME_FORMATTER` and throws UnsupportedTemporalTypeException (ObjectSerializer.kt:520-527), and no LocalTime KSerializer is registered in the module (~:990), so a time model field cannot serialize either. csharp: TimeOnly -> HH:mm:ss, fraction dropped (ObjectSerializer.cs:158). php: time maps to \DateTimeImmutable and stringify formats it as a full RFC 3339 date-time (ObjectSerializer.php:262, DATE_TIME_FORMAT). python: isoformat(timespec=seconds), dropped (object_serializer.py:586). ruby: Tod::TimeOfDay strftime('%H:%M:%S'), dropped (object_serializer.rb:190, 287). node: Temporal.PlainTime.toString(), minimal digits kept (object-serializer.ts:439, 931). rust: chrono::NaiveTime Display, fraction kept. elixir: Time.truncate(:second), dropped (object_serializer.ex:265, 386). go, dart, swift: time maps to String, caller supplies text.
canonical: A `format: time` value is written as `HH:mm:ss` (no date, no offset); when the millisecond part is non-zero it is written as `HH:mm:ss.SSS` (exactly three digits, sub-millisecond digits truncated, never rounded). Same form for path/query/header/cookie params and JSON bodies. Parsing accepts HH:mm:ss with an optional fraction. go/dart/swift pass the caller's string through (their type is String).
rationale: RFC 3339 partial-time; the whole-second form matches every spec example and is what 4 SDKs already emit, so strict-pattern servers keep working (criterion c). Keeping milliseconds avoids the silent fraction loss of csharp/python/ruby/elixir and matches java/node/rust (b), capped at ms like the date-time canon. Kotlin throwing a raw java.time exception violates the AGENTS error contract (a). php can special-case via the schemaType tag it already passes (`\DateTimeImmutable` identifies time, `|date` identifies date).
alternatives: Seconds only everywhere: rejected, silently truncates fractions that java/node/rust preserve. Always .SSS like date-time: rejected, changes the common whole-second form that strict servers expect and that spec examples show. Verbatim minimal digits (java/node today): rejected, not byte-identical across languages. Caveat: ruby's tod gem must carry sub-second values; if Tod::TimeOfDay cannot, ruby becomes a documented FORCED seconds-only exception.
risk: Public wire change for csharp/python/ruby/elixir (adds a fraction when present) and java/node/rust (ms cap). php body path needs a DateTimeNormalizer format per time property.

canonical: The four languages that model bare `type: number` as a decimal (java, kotlin, csharp, node) are exact in both directions: decode keeps the numeric text, encode writes an unquoted JSON number in PLAIN notation (no exponent), and a non-numeric string is rejected. python is exact on decode (Decimal parsed from the text) and a FORCED float-widening on encode (pydantic/stdlib json cannot emit a raw Decimal without a dependency), documented as such. rationale: A documented promise of exact decimals (criterion a: README/AGENTS) that is silently broken on decode is a silent data change on money-like values (c). Python encode genuinely cannot (named feature: pydantic-core's JSON serializer has no raw-number type) so it is documented FORCED rather than forced into a hack.
alternatives: Only correct the docs and move python/node to the lossy list: defensible and zero risk, rejected because java/kotlin/csharp prove exactness is achievable and node's rawJSON encode path already exists. Add a decimal dependency to python: rejected (criterion d).
risk: python parse_float=Decimal turns every JSON float into Decimal, so LaxFloat (format float/double) needs a Decimal->float widening BeforeValidator and free-form/additionalProperties numbers become Decimal in memory; the json.dumps default=str fallback would then quote them, so add a Decimal->float default. title: Declared-charset decoding: documented minimum set plus lenient UTF-8 fallback that always yields a valid string
current_state: Re-checked. dart now decodes latin1/ascii/windows-1252 (via a table)/utf-16 BOM-aware, anything else falls back to lenient UTF-8 with U+FFFD (abstract_api_client.dart:706-748). elixir now has windows-1252 (default_api_client.ex:586-599), latin1, utf-16/32, but any unknown label returns the RAW body bytes (decode_text_body :480-530), which can be an invalid UTF-8 string. go supports utf-8/ascii/latin1/windows-1252/utf-16 and returns string(body) raw for anything else (default_api_client.go:526-552), also possibly invalid UTF-8. swift decodes about 16 labels and falls back leniently with U+FFFD. java/kotlin (JVM charsets), csharp (CodePages), python, ruby, php (mbstring), node (TextDecoder) and rust (encoding_rs) decode any registered charset (ledger audit).
canonical: Minimum guaranteed set in every SDK: utf-8, us-ascii, iso-8859-1, windows-1252, utf-16 (BOM-aware; bare label big-endian without BOM), utf-16le/be. Languages with a charset registry (java, kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, php, node, rust) decode everything it knows; languages without one (go, dart, elixir, swift) decode the minimum set and, for any other label (shift_jis, iso-8859-2, ...), fall back to a lenient UTF-8 decode that substitutes U+FFFD, so the returned string is always valid. title: Response headers returned to the caller drop Content-Encoding and Content-Length whenever the body was decoded
current_state: Re-checked rust: after decompress_body succeeds it removes content-encoding and content-length from the returned map (default_api_client.rs:457-465). csharp: AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.All (DefaultApiClient.cs:146) makes HttpClient strip both from Content.Headers before the SDK sees them. swift: URLSession decodes gzip/deflate itself and on Apple strips Content-Encoding; on Linux the header survives (AGENTS.md notes this). java, kotlin, python, ruby, php, node (fetch), dart, go (Accept-Encoding set explicitly) and elixir hand the wire content-encoding and the compressed content-length through ApiHttpResponse.headers and ApiException.responseHeaders (ledger audit, not re-run here).
canonical: ApiHttpResponse.headers and ApiException.responseHeaders describe the body the caller receives: whenever the SDK (or its runtime) decoded a non-identity Content-Encoding, Content-Encoding and Content-Length are removed from the returned headers. An identity or absent Content-Encoding leaves both untouched.
rationale: This is what the mainstream HTTP clients do when they decompress transparently (Go net/http, OkHttp, Apache HttpClient, .NET, Apple URLSession, reqwest, which the rust code comment already cites), so csharp/swift/rust are right and the nine are the minority (b). A caller comparing Content-Length with the body length then never sees a mismatch (c). Preserving wire headers is not reachable: csharp and swift cannot restore headers their runtime already removed (named features: HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression and URLSession), whereas stripping is feasible everywhere (d).
alternatives: Preserve wire headers everywhere (rust stops stripping): rejected, csharp and swift would become forced exceptions and the preserved Content-Length would be wrong for the delivered body. Leave it as documented runtime-dependent behaviour: viable and cheaper, but keeps a caller-visible difference with no forcing reason.
risk: Low, header contents only. Do not strip when the SDK did not decode (identity, or the AGENTS-documented node/swift/dart-web pass-through of an unknown coding), and strip case-insensitively.
